description: We are curious and enthusiastic students who are passionate about science and discovering new things. We are ready to take on challenges, try new ideas, and show what we can do. We want to learn, create, and contribute to science through our project.Join our team if you are friendly, responsible, creative, and willing to learn. We welcome everyone’s ideas!
summary:
Bridging Tradition, Technology and Space Exploration

Our project combines traditional Vietnamese shadow puppetry with an interactive learning website to bring space science closer to young learners.

Through the story of NASA's Opportunity rover, we turn an incredible Mars exploration mission into a creative and inspiring learning experience. By connecting traditional art with modern technology, we aim to preserve cultural heritage while encouraging scientific curiosity.

Designed for students in Grades 6–12, our website offers real NASA images, fascinating facts, mission timelines and interactive activities. Students can explore Mars, discover Opportunity's achievements and learn at their own pace.

The entire platform is completely free and easy to access. We also promote environmental awareness through digital resources and reusable or recycled materials for our performances.
details:
Opportunity Rover Learning Platform is a free website that teaches students in grades 6–12 about NASA’s Opportunity rover: Opportunity. Students choose their grade and one of five languages: Vietnamese, English, Chinese, Japanese or Korean. The site then tells Oppy’s story in short chapters:

 

1. A 3D model of the rover that students can rotate;

2. The 3D journey from Earth to Mars;

3. Oppy’s discoveries;

4. A year-by-year timeline;

5. A map of its 45 km route on Mars;

6. Why contact was lost in the 2018 dust storm;

7. A glossary and a quiz.

 

In the “Drive Oppy” game, students drive the rover to three real rocks studied in Eagle Crater in 2004 while managing its solar-powered battery. Finishing the mission unlocks a printable certificate.

 

What benefits does it have?

Students learn real NASA mission science in their own language and at their own level. There are three levels: Explorer (grades 6–7), Young Scientist (grades 8–9) and Mission Engineer (grades 10–12). It is free, needs no sign-up and nothing to install, and works on both computers and phones. Teachers can use it in class, and students can keep learning at home.

 

What is the intended impact?

We want students in Vietnam and across Asia, who rarely find space science written for them, to feel that Mars exploration is within their reach. We hope it encourages more of them to choose STEM.

 

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did you use?

Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no outside libraries.

All 3D graphics (the rover, rocket, Earth, Mars and the driving game) are drawn with our own code on HTML Canvas 2D, so the site works even on computers without WebGL.

A rover model simplified from NASA 3D Resources.

Photos from NASA/JPL.

Fonts from Google Fonts.

Hosting on Netlify.

No special hardware is needed.

We used an AI assistant to help with parts of the coding and translation, and our team reviewed and tested all the content.

 

How is your project creative?

Students do not just read about Opportunity: they become its drivers. They use the real rock targets, avoid sand traps and wait for the solar panels to recharge, just as the real team had to. A passing dust devil can even blow the panels clean, as really happened on Mars. The design uses the colors of Mars itself: rust-brown ground, a butterscotch daytime sky and blue sunsets.

 

What factors did your team consider?

Wording that suits each age.

Scientific accuracy, with facts checked against NASA and JPL sources.

Accessibility: keyboard and touch controls, screen-reader labels and reduced motion.

Older or low-power devices, which is why the 3D runs without WebGL.

Privacy: there are no accounts, and progress is saved only in the student’s own browser.
